The year I turned twenty-five, I got promoted and stopped sleeping. I told myself it was normal: new role, more pressure. My sister finally said, "You go to the dentist twice a year for your teeth. When did you last check on your head?"
I laughed, but it stuck. I found Nirmala through a clinic my company's insurance covered. She was a counsellor, not a psychiatrist; I'd checked the difference first, because I didn't think I needed medicine, just someone to talk to.
The first session I kept saying "I'm fine, just stressed." Nirmala asked, "What does stressed feel like in your body?" I didn't know. I'd never noticed.
We met every two weeks for six months. I learned to spot the tight jaw before the panic, and to say no to one extra project. Now I go once every couple of months, like servicing a scooter. I'm Kashish. It's not a crisis thing. It's maintenance.

qa.a: Every two weeks for six months.

qa.q: How did Kashish feel in the first session?
qa.a: Kashish felt guarded and unsure, insisting on being fine and not knowing what stress felt like in the body.

qa.q: What did Kashish do well in choosing appropriate help?
qa.a: Kashish checked the difference between a counsellor and a psychiatrist and chose based on the need, using a clinic covered by insurance.

qa.q: How might Kashish's sister feel seeing therapy become routine?
qa.a: The sister probably feels relieved and glad the dentist comparison helped make it ordinary.

grounding: Shows a young adult treating counselling as ordinary maintenance and choosing the right kind of help.

Employee wellbeing note. Anand, HR wellbeing lead.
Divyansh, 24, came to ask about the company's counselling benefit, very quietly, as if asking about something illegal. He said his father had called therapy "for weak people".
I explained what we offer: six free sessions with a licensed counsellor, fully confidential; a peer-support circle on Thursdays run by trained colleagues; and, if needed, a referral to a psychiatrist through our insurance. I told him many people use it for ordinary things: stress, a breakup, a move.
He chose the peer circle first, to test the water. After three weeks, he booked counselling too.
Last week he told me he'd mentioned it to his father. "He didn't say much. But he asked if it helped." Divyansh looked lighter.
Plan: keep running the circle and share, anonymously, how many staff used the service this year, so it feels normal.

qa.a: Six free sessions with a licensed counsellor.

qa.a: It suggests Divyansh felt embarrassed and ashamed, as if seeking help were something to hide.

qa.a: It let him start with the least intimidating option, the peer circle, and move to counselling once he felt ready.

Maria had come back to her small hometown in Goa to teach at the village school. At church, she was "Aunty Rosa's good daughter" who sang in the choir. At weekends, she ran a campaign against illegal sand mining on the river, which some parishioners' relatives profited from.
She felt like two people. At Sunday Mass, she avoided eyes. At protest meetings, she avoided mentioning church.
Her friend Bhavna, a fellow teacher, asked, "Why do you keep them separate? Doesn't your faith say something about caring for creation?"
Maria thought about the old priest's sermons about the river as a gift. That evening she spoke to him. He listened, then asked her to speak about the river at the parish youth meeting.
She was nervous, and some families were cold afterwards. But for the first time, singing in the choir and standing at the riverbank felt like parts of the same person.

In Buenos Aires, Alejandro had two job offers: a stable bank job and a small start-up building farm software. He was twenty-five and had some savings.
His girlfriend Valentina suggested they write it down. What did he know? The bank's salary, the start-up's smaller pay with shares, that he loved the product. What didn't he know? Whether the start-up would survive.
"Guess," she said. "Out of ten start-ups like this, how many last three years?"
"Maybe three."
"And if it fails, what happens to you?"
"I'd have learned a lot, and I could find another job."
He took the start-up, with an agreement to review after one year. Eighteen months later it shut down. He was sad, but not bitter. "It was a good decision that turned out badly," he told Valentina. "Those aren't the same thing." He started at a bigger farm-tech firm a month later.

qa.a: He listed what he knew and didn't, estimated the odds, checked what failure would cost him, and set a review point.

At the municipal disaster-management office in Chennai, Naveen, twenty-six, had to recommend by 6 p.m. whether to evacuate a low-lying settlement. The forecast said heavy rain was "likely", but the models disagreed on how heavy.
His senior, Siddharth, asked, "What happens if we evacuate and it doesn't flood? What happens if we don't and it does?"
Naveen wrote it out. Evacuating: families lose a night's sleep and some wages, and trust drops if it's a false alarm. Not evacuating: people might drown. The costs weren't equal.
At 4 p.m., a new update raised the rain estimate. Naveen updated his view. He recommended evacuation.
The rain came, but less than feared. Some residents grumbled. Siddharth said, "We'd make the same call again. Explain it to them honestly." Naveen went to the relief centre the next morning and explained the forecast to anyone who asked.

qa.q: By what time did Naveen have to make his recommendation?
qa.a: By 6 p.m.

qa.q: How might Naveen have felt when some residents grumbled?
qa.a: Naveen probably felt uncomfortable and a bit defensive, but reassured by Siddharth that the decision was right.

qa.q: What made Naveen's decision sound even though the flood was smaller?
qa.a: He compared the unequal costs of each mistake, updated his view with the new forecast, and explained the reasoning openly afterwards.

qa.q: How might the residents see the evacuation after Naveen explained the forecast?
qa.a: Some might still be annoyed, but many could understand and trust the office more for being honest.

grounding: Illustrates a young official deciding under uncertainty, updating on new information and accepting outcome variance.

You asked, Mahima, what it's like leading the team that brought AI into our customer support. I'm Rekha, and the honest answer is: it's not the tool that's hard, it's staying responsible.
When we started, the AI answered customer emails directly. It was fast. Then one day it told a customer they'd get a full refund they weren't entitled to. Another day, it invented a delivery date. The customers were angry at us, not at the AI.

Two years ago I had eighty-three apps on my phone. I checked it one hundred and fifty times a day; the phone told me so. I felt busy and scattered all the time, and I couldn't read a book for more than five minutes.
My friend Rajni had quietly deleted most of hers and seemed calmer. I asked how. She said, "I didn't quit. I chose."

Sarika here. The app audit is done.
A month ago Aparna Didi challenged me: write down every app I opened and how I felt after. I thought it would be boring. It was shocking.
Short-video app: forty minutes a day, felt worse every time. News app: checked eleven times a day, learned nothing new after the first. Shopping app: opened when bored, bought things I didn't need.
Apps I felt better after: my language-learning one, the one where I call Nani, my notes app.
So I deleted the video and shopping apps. I moved news to one check at lunch, from one proper newspaper site. I set my phone to greyscale after nine.
It's not perfect. I reinstalled the video app on day twelve and deleted it again on day thirteen. But I feel like the phone is mine again.

qa.q: How many times a day did Sarika check the news app?
qa.a: Eleven times a day.

qa.q: How does Sarika feel at the end of the audit?
qa.a: Sarika feels calmer and more in control, like the phone is Sarika's own again, despite a slip on day twelve.

qa.q: Why was tracking how each app made Sarika feel a useful method?
qa.a: It showed which apps served Sarika and which drained time or mood, so choices were based on evidence, not habit.

qa.q: How might Aparna Didi feel reading this diary entry?
qa.a: Aparna Didi would probably feel proud and pleased that the challenge worked.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult auditing technology use and choosing an information diet deliberately.

At the bank branch in Pune, Tanuja, twenty-six, sat across from Kalyani, the home-loan officer. Everyone in her office was buying flats, and her parents kept saying rent was "money thrown away".
Tanuja expected a sales pitch. Instead, Kalyani drew two columns. Renting: flexibility to move for work, no big down payment, landlord handles major repairs. Buying: stability and an asset, but a large loan for many years, maintenance, and less freedom to move.
"It depends on your job, your plans and how long you'd stay," Kalyani said. "And whether you have insurance and an emergency fund first."
Tanuja admitted she might move cities in two years. Kalyani nodded. "Then think carefully. I can explain our loans, but for your whole plan, see a certified financial planner."
Tanuja left with a brochure and a list of questions. She felt oddly relieved not to have signed anything.

qa.q: What did Kalyani say Tanuja should have before buying?
qa.a: Insurance and an emergency fund.

qa.q: How did Tanuja feel leaving the bank?
qa.a: Tanuja felt oddly relieved not to have signed anything, after arriving under pressure.

qa.q: Why was Kalyani's approach helpful rather than pushy?
qa.a: She laid out the trade-offs of renting and buying, linked them to Tanuja's plans, and pointed her to a certified planner for the full picture.

qa.q: How might Tanuja's parents react to her not buying yet?
qa.a: Her parents might be disappointed at first, but could understand if she explains the possible move and the planner's advice.

grounding: Shows a young adult comparing renting and buying with a bank officer's balanced explanation and a referral to a qualified planner.

Dear Vandana Akka,
You're the only person in the family who works in finance, so I'm writing before I meet the adviser next week.
Here's what I've understood so far, and please tell me if I've got it wrong.
Health insurance: my company gives some cover, but it ends if I leave the job, so I'm looking at a separate policy too.
Term life insurance: it pays out only if I die during the term; it's for people who depend on me. Amma does, partly.
Retirement: starting early matters because money has more time to grow, even small amounts.
What I don't know: how much cover is "enough", and which retirement options fit someone like me.
I've written down my income, rent, what I send Amma, and my savings, so the adviser can see the real picture.
Is there anything else I should ask?
Ira

Mohit, you asked on the podcast why I, at twenty-six, haven't bought a flat when all my friends have. I'm Leela, and here's my honest answer.
I sat down with a financial planner last year. We compared buying in my city with renting. For me, the loan would take a very large part of my salary for twenty years. My job may take me to another city. And I had no proper health insurance or emergency fund yet.
So I decided to rent for now. I sorted out insurance first. I started a small monthly retirement contribution, because the planner showed me how starting at twenty-six versus thirty-six changes things.
My aunt still says rent is wasted money. Maybe for her it was. For me, flexibility is worth something.
I might buy in five years. Or I might not. But it will be a choice, not a panic.

qa.q: What did Leela sort out first?
qa.a: Insurance.

qa.q: How does Leela seem to feel about the aunt's comments?
qa.a: Leela seems calm and a bit amused, secure in those reasons even when others disagree.

qa.q: What made Leela's decision thoughtful?
qa.a: Leela compared renting and buying with a qualified planner against Leela's own job, security and goals, and put insurance first.

qa.q: How might Leela's friends who bought flats see Leela's choice?
qa.a: Some might think Leela is missing out, while others may respect that Leela's situation is different from theirs.

grounding: Shows a young adult comparing renting and buying, prioritising insurance and starting retirement saving with professional advice.

At the tech company's Gurugram office, the lunch table talk was always about upgrades: new phones, new cars, weekend trips. Devika had just got a raise. Her colleague Yamini said, "Now you can finally get a decent car. Everyone judges the one you park."
Devika felt the pull. Her old hatchback looked shabby next to the new SUVs in the basement.
That evening she sat with her notebook. Her rent had gone up. She was helping her brother with college. She had wanted to build savings to take a course abroad someday.
She asked herself: would a new car make her life better, or just make her look better at the lunch table?
She kept the hatchback and got it serviced and cleaned. She did book one weekend trip with friends, which she'd been dreaming of. At lunch, when Yamini asked, Devika said, "Car's fine. I'm saving for something bigger." Nobody cared as much as she'd feared.

qa.q: What did Yamini say Devika could finally get?
qa.a: A decent car.

qa.q: How did Devika feel about her old hatchback in the office basement?
qa.a: Devika felt self-conscious and tempted, as it looked shabby next to the new SUVs.

qa.q: Which question helped Devika separate needs from image?
qa.a: Whether a new car would make her life better or just make her look better, which helped her choose her own priorities.

qa.q: How might Yamini see Devika's answer at lunch?
qa.a: Yamini probably didn't think much of it, showing that the judgement Devika feared was smaller than expected.

grounding: Illustrates a young professional resisting status spending after a raise and aligning expenses with her priorities.

Hi Bhupen,
You asked how I avoided "going crazy" after the raise. Honestly, I almost did.
The week the raise came through, I nearly signed up for a bigger flat, a gym membership that costs more than my old rent, and a new phone. I'd scrolled through colleagues' posts and felt behind.
Then I remembered my father, who got a promotion when I was ten and moved us to a nicer house, and then was stressed about bills for years.
So I made a rule for myself, which I'm not saying anyone else should follow: when income goes up, I first decide what I'm saving toward, then allow one thing that really improves my life. I chose a better mattress because I sleep badly.
The flat can wait. The phone works. I feel calmer than I did with the fancy stuff in my cart.
Nandini

qa.q: What did Nandini choose as the one thing that improves life?
qa.a: A better mattress.

qa.q: How did Nandini feel after scrolling through colleagues' posts?
qa.a: Nandini felt behind and tempted to spend on a bigger flat, gym and phone.

qa.q: What memory helped Nandini avoid lifestyle inflation, and why?
qa.a: Remembering Nandini's father's stress after upgrading their house showed that raising spending with income can bring worry, not comfort.

qa.q: How might Bhupen see Nandini's approach?
qa.a: Bhupen might find it sensible and calming, and think about Bhupen's own spending.

grounding: Shows a young professional avoiding lifestyle inflation after a raise by separating real needs from image.

Sarika, you asked on the show about my wedding. I'm Nitin, and here's the story.
Everyone in my family expected a big wedding: three functions, five hundred guests, the works. My fiancée and I had good jobs, so relatives assumed we'd "show it". Some suggested a loan.
We sat down one night and listed what mattered to us: our families, a few close friends, good food, and starting married life without debt. The big wedding didn't fit most of that.
Telling my parents was hard. My mother cried and said people would think we were struggling. I said, "Let them. We're not."
We had one function, a hundred and fifty guests, a lovely lunch. Some relatives grumbled. But no one remembers the size now. What I remember is my grandmother dancing.
We used what we'd saved for a small home deposit instead.

qa.q: How many guests came to Nitin's wedding?
qa.a: A hundred and fifty guests.

qa.q: How did Nitin's mother feel about the smaller wedding?
qa.a: Nitin's mother felt upset, crying, worried people would think the couple was struggling.

qa.q: What helped Nitin and the fiancée resist status spending?
qa.a: They listed what really mattered to them and saw a big, debt-funded wedding didn't match, then held firm kindly with family.

qa.q: How might the relatives who grumbled see it years later?
qa.a: They may barely remember the size, as Nitin says, while the couple still benefits from avoiding debt.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult choosing a smaller wedding to avoid status spending and debt despite family expectations.

Thursday
Divyansh writing. Went to my first ward committee meeting tonight, in the community hall behind the vegetable market. Dhruv from the flat downstairs dragged me along. I expected boring speeches.
Instead there was a real fight. The corporation plans to widen the main road, which means cutting the footpath and some trees. Shopkeepers want more parking. Parents want a safe footpath for kids walking to school. Both had a point.
The ward officer explained the budget: they can't do everything. Widening helps traffic; footpaths help safety; trees help heat.
Dhruv and I spoke for three minutes, suggesting a narrower widening with a protected footpath and relocated parking. I was nervous but clear.
They're collecting written suggestions till the 15th. I'm going to write ours up properly, with photos of kids walking in the road. First time I've felt like my city is partly mine.

qa.q: What does the corporation plan to widen?
qa.a: The main road.

qa.q: How did Divyansh feel speaking at the meeting?
qa.a: Divyansh felt nervous but clear, and later felt that the city was partly Divyansh's own.

qa.q: What made Divyansh's participation constructive?
qa.a: Divyansh listened to both sides, understood the budget limits, and proposed a compromise backed by evidence.

qa.q: How might the shopkeepers see the suggestion of relocated parking?
qa.a: The shopkeepers might be partly satisfied, since parking stays, even if not right outside their shops.

grounding: Shows a young adult understanding a public policy trade-off and participating constructively in local governance.

At the gram sabha in their village in Rajasthan, Suraj, twenty-five, sat on the mat near the back. He'd come home after working in Jaipur and wanted to understand how the village budget was decided.
The sarpanch announced the year's funds. The choice was between repairing the road to the highway and building a new water tank. Voices rose. Farmers needed the road for markets. Women spoke about walking far for water in summer.
Suraj's friend Farhan, who worked at the panchayat office, whispered, "Most years, the loudest group wins."
Suraj stood up, heart pounding. "Can we see what each costs and how many families each helps? Maybe the tank first, and a road patch before the monsoon?"
The secretary read out figures. The meeting went on another hour. They voted: tank now, road repairs next year, a patch before the rains.
Walking home, Farhan said, "You should come every time." Suraj thought he might.

qa.q: What were the two choices for the village funds?
qa.a: Repairing the road to the highway or building a new water tank.

qa.q: How did Suraj feel when he stood up to speak?
qa.a: Suraj felt nervous, heart pounding, speaking up at the gram sabha.

qa.q: What made Suraj's contribution constructive?
qa.a: Suraj asked for costs and numbers of families helped, then suggested a phased plan balancing both needs.

qa.q: How might the women who spoke about water see the decision?
qa.a: The women probably feel relieved and heard, since the tank comes first.

grounding: Shows a young adult participating constructively in local governance and weighing a public policy trade-off.
